Tischler and Piet Maes The citation for this ICTV Report chapter is the summary published as: Bradfute, S. B., Calisher, C. H., Klempa, B., Klingström, J., Kuhn, J. H., Laenen, L., Tischler, N. D., & Maes, P. (2024). ICTV Virus Taxonomy Profile: Hantaviridae 2024, Journal of General Virology 105, 001975 Corresponding author: Piet Maes ( [email protected] ) Edited by: Holly Hughes and Evelien Adriaenssens Posted: March 2024, updated June 2024 Summary Hantaviridae is a family for negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes of about 10.5–14.6 kb (Table 1 Hantaviridae ). The family includes eight genera ( Actinovirus and Percilovirus (subfamily Actantavirinae ), Agnathovirus (subfamily Agantavirinae ), Loanvirus , Mobatvirus , Orthohantavirus and Thottimvirus (subfamily Mammantavirinae ), and Reptillovirus (subfamily Repantavirinae ). These viruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by small mammals, but also by fish and reptiles. Several orthohantaviruses can infect humans, causing mild, severe, and sometimes-fatal diseases. Hantavirids produce enveloped virions containing three single-stranded RNA segments with open reading frames (ORFs) that encode a nucleoprotein (N), a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Table 1 Hantaviridae. Characteristics of members of the family Hantaviridae. Characteristic Description* Example Hantaan virus (S segment: M14626; M segment: M14627; L segment: X55901), species Orthohantavirus hantanense Virion Enveloped, pleomorphic virions 80–160 nm in diameter with heterodimeric surface spikes Genome Three single-stranded RNA molecules (segments): small (S; 1.0–3.0 kb), medium (M; 3.4–4.8 kb), and large (L; 5.3–6.8 kb) Replication Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes containing anti-genomic RNA serve as coding templates for synthesis of genomic RNA Translation Proteins are produced from capped and non-polyadenylated mRNAs. The 5′-cap structure is obtained via cap-snatching from cellular mRNAs Host range Fish (actinoviruses, agnathoviruses, perciloviruses), mammals (orthohantaviruses), and reptiles (reptilloviruses) Taxonomy Realm Riboviria , kingdom Orthornavirae , phylum Negarnaviricota , class Bunyaviricetes , order Elliovirales ; the family includes four subfamilies, eight genera, and 55 species * mostly based on experiments with mammalian orthohantaviruses Viruses assigned to each of the seven genera form genus-specifc monophyletic clades based on phylogenetic analysis of concatenated L protein/RdRP, glycoprotein and N sequences. Viruses from all seven genera share one or more of the following characteristics: (i) enveloped pleomorphic virions; (ii) tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome without polyadenylated tracts at the 3′-end; (iii) genomic sequence complementarity at the 5′- and 3′-ends; and (iv) capped but not polyadenylated virus mRNAs ( Maes et al., 2004 ). Piscine Hosts Genus Actinovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian (percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) fish. Genus Agnathovirus . Viruses in this genus infect agnathan (myxinid) fish. Genus Percilovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian ( gobiid, lophiid ) fish. Mammalian Hosts Genus Loanvirus. Viruses in this genus infect rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly nycterid bats and possibly murid rodents. Genus Mobatvirus. Viruses in this genus infect emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid and possibly molossid, and vespertillionid bats and soricid and talpid eulipotyphla. Genus Orthohantavirus. Viruses assigned to this genus infect soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Genus Thottimvirus. Viruses in this genus infect soricid and possibly talpid eulipotyphla. Reptilian Hosts Genus Reptillovirus . Viruses in this genus infect gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles. Virion Morphology Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Physicochemical and physical properties Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Nucleic acid Hantavirids have tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes (S, M, and L segments). The viral mRNAs are not polyadenylated and contain a 5′-methylated cap and several non-templated nucleotides at the 5′-end that are derived from host cell mRNAs via cap snatching ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Further information is only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Proteins Hantavirids typically express three structural proteins. The most abundant structural protein in a hantavirion is N, which encapsidates the hantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , are produced from GPC and mediate entry of hantavirions ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Spiropoulou 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Lipids Not reported but are likely derived from the Golgi apparatus and/or the host cell plasma membrane and therefore likely composed of phospholipids, glycolipids, fatty acids, and sterols. Carbohydrates Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Genome organization and replication S RNA encodes N and in some viruses NSs ( Jääskeläinen et al., 2007 , Vera-Otarola et al., 2012 ), M RNA encodes GPC, and the L RNA encodes L with its RdRP, helicase, and endonuclease domains ( Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 ) (Figure 1 Hantaviridae ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Figure 1 Hantaviridae . Genome organization of representative hantaviruses. The 5′- and 3′- ends of all segments are complementary at their termini, likely promoting the formation of panhandle RNP complexes within the virion . GPC , glycoprotein precursor gene; L , large (protein) gene; N , nucleoprotein gene. Biology Hantavirids have been found in actinopterygian (gobiid, lophiid, percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) and agnathan (myxinid) fish; in emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid, rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly molossid and nycterid bats; in soricid and talpid eulipotyphla; in muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents; in gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles; and potentially in coleopteran and plectopteran insects (see genus pages for details). Only orthohantaviruses are known to cause diseases (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Antigenicity Systematic antigenicity studies have only been reported for orthohantaviruses (see Orthohantavirus genus page). species demarcation criteria The availability of at least coding-complete sequences of all three genome segments may be sufficient for hantavirid classification in the absence of a cultured isolate. Demarcation of genera is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Hantaviridae: current classification and future perspectives, Viruses, 11, 9, e0788">Laenen et al., 2019 ). DEmARC analysis gave a frequency distribution of Pairwise Evolutionary Distance (PED) values of which the threshold of 0.1 gave an optimal clustering cost of zero and is used as the hantavirid species demarcation criterium. Genera are demarked by a PED-value threshold of 0.95 and subfamilies are demarcated based on their distinct clustering in a Bayesian maximum clade credibility tree and a PED-value threshold of 3.5. Relationships within the family Phylogenetic relationships across the family have been estimated using Bayesian maximum clade credibility trees generated from complete N, GPC, and L amino-acid sequences; similar topologies are obtained with concatenated N and GPC sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Figure 2 Hantaviridae . Maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree inferred using IQ-TREE. The tree was constructed based on 53 concatenated S and M segment (amino acid) sequences using the LG+R9 model of sequence evolution. Branch lengths represent the estimated number of substitutions per site. Bootstrap support values (>70%) are indicated at nodes, reflecting the degree of confidence in the branching pattern. Relationships with other taxa Hantavirids are closely related to bunyaviral crulivirids, fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids ( Wolf et al., 2018 , Herath et al., 2020 ). Using the Master Species List Using the Virus Metadata Resource Using the Find the Species tool Using the ICTV Report Webinar Webinar on Virus Taxonomy Webinar on Finding Information GitHub Repository Zenodo Repository Email ICTV Help ‏‏‎ ‎ ICTV Report Book: Hantaviridae Family: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Actantavirinae Genus: Actinovirus Genus: Percilovirus Subfamily: Agantavirinae Genus: Agnathovirus Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Loanvirus Genus: Mobatvirus Genus: Orthohantavirus Genus: Thottimvirus Subfamily: Repantavirinae Genus: Reptillovirus Authors: Hantaviridae Citation: Hantaviridae References: Hantaviridae Resources: Hantaviridae Species List: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Orthohantavirus Distinguishing features Sixty different viruses are classified in the genus Orthohantavius. These viruses typically infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease in humans ( Schmaljohn and Hjelle 1997 , Jonsson et al., 2010 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 , Vial et al., 2023 ). Virion Morphology Orthohantavirions are pleomorphic in shape, mostly spherical of 80–160 nm in diameter ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ), and surrounded by a membrane envelope that is decorated with glycoprotein (GP) spikes composed of G N and G C subunits (Figure 1 Orthohantavirus ). The virion envelope is 5 nm thick and is decorated with square shaped spikes, consisting of tetrameric G N -G C heterodimers, which protrude 10 nM from the membrane forming a surface lattice of local symmetry interrupted by empty membrane spots ( Hung et al., 1983 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Parvate et al., 2019 , Serris et al., 2020 , Guardado-Calvo and Rey 2021 ). Isolated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are composed of individual segment genomic RNA encapsidated by nucleoprotein (N) ( Tao et al., 1987 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Hepojoki et al., 2012 , Guo et al., 2016 , Arragain et al., 2019 ). Virions assemble and bud from the Golgi complex or cell surface membranes, depending on the virus ( Goldsmith et al., 1995 , Parvate et al., 2019 ). Figure 1 Orthohantavirus. A, B) Electron micrographs of Tula virus particles adapted from ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ). C) Schematic illustration of an orthohantavirus particle. Shown is a spherical and enveloped (grey) particle with glycoprotein spikes (G N yellow, G C blue) inserted in a bilaminar lipid envelope. The S (small), M (medium), and L (large) RNP (ribonucleoprotein) complexes inside the particle consist of N (nucleoprotein, green) and L (large protein, pink). ViralZone image reproduced courtesy of SwissBioPics. Physicochemical and physical properties Virion buoyant densities in sucrose and CsCl are 1.15–1.18 ( White et al., 1982 ) and 1.20–1.21 g cm −3 , respectively ( Schmaljohn et al., 1983 ). Virions are sensitive to chemical inactivation with, for instance, methanol, paraformaldehyde, acetone/methanol, N -ethylmaleimide or detergents, as well as physical methods such as heat, gamma irradiation or UV irradiation ( Kraus et al., 2005 , Strandin et al., 2011 , Elveborg et al., 2022 ). Nucleic acid Orthohantavirus genomes are linear tri-segmented RNA molecules of negative polarity. The genomes are about 11.1–12.3 kb in length (small [S] segment: 1.2–2.1 kb; medium [M] segment: 3.4–3.8 kb; large [L] segment: 6.5–6.6 kb). Proteins Orthohantaviruses typically express three structural proteins (Table 1 Orthohantavirus ). The most abundant structural protein in an orthohantavirion is N, which encapsidates the orthohantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , mediate virion entry. G N and G C and non-structural proteins are encoded as a precursor polyprotein. Table 1 Orthohantavirus . Location and function of orthohantavirus structural proteins. Protein Location, mass, and function Reference Nucleoprotein (N) Structural virion protein (about 48 kD). Oligomerizes and encapsidates orthohantaviral genomic segments and hence component of RNPs. Binds to L and G N ( Mir et al., 2010 , Reuter and Krüger 2018 , Arragain et al., 2019 ) Nonstructural protein (NSs) Non-structural protein encoded by some orhtohantaviruses. Has type I interferon inhibitory activity. May occur as multiple isoforms. ( Vera-Otarola et al., 2020 , Binder et al., 2021 ) Glycoprotein (GP) Structural virion protein consisting of two subunits (G N : about 70-75 kD, G C : about 50-55 kD). Produced via proteolytic cleavage from the genome-encoded precursor GPC. Projects from virion membranes as tetrameric GP spikes composed of G N and G C heterodimers. GP mediates cell- receptor binding; as a class II fusion machine it induces virion-cell membrane fusion and, thereby cell entry. G N binds to N and RNA ( Spiropoulou et al., 2003 , Tischler et al., 2005 , Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014 , Li et al., 2016 , Willensky et al., 2016 , Rissanen et al., 2017 , Zhu et al., 2018 , Bignon et al., 2019 , Sperber et al., 2019 ) Large protein (L) Structural virion protein (246 kD) with RdRP, helicase, and endoribonuclease domains. Component of the RNP inside virions. Binds to N and RNA. Oligomerizes and mediates transcription and replication of viral RNA segments. Mediates cap-snatching for viral mRNA capping. ( Kukkonen et al., 2005 , Cheng et al., 2014 , Rothenberger et al., 2016 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Durieux Trouilleton et al., 2023 ) Genome organization and replication The orthohantavirus genome consists of three negative-sense RNA molecules, termed S (small), M (medium), and L (large) (Figure 2 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 2 Orthohantavirus. Schematic representation of orthohantavirus genome organization. Orthohantavirus genomic segments assume circular forms via non-covalent binding of complementary and highly conserved 3′- and 5′-terminal sequences. Genomic segment reassortment mostly occurs among viruses belonging to the same species but interspecies reassortment likely occurs occasionally ( Klempa 2018 , Petazzi et al., 2021 ). Orthohantavirus infection starts with virion attachment, mediated by G N and G C , to cell-surface attachment factors and entry via the endosomal route ( Shtanko et al., 2014 ) (Figure 3 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 3 Orthohantavirus . Lifecycle of orthohantaviruses. (1) Virion attachment; (2) virion uptake; (3) virion-cell membrane fusion; (4) transcription; (5) translation; (6) replication; (7) virion assembly; and (8) virion egress. After engaging a cellular receptor, protocadherin 1 in the case of American orthohantaviruses, virion-membrane fusion results in early or late endosomal release, depending on the virus, of the virion RNP complex into the cytoplasm in a pH-dependent manner ( Jangra et al., 2018 , Mittler et al., 2019 , Torriani et al., 2019 , Dieterle et al., 2021 ). During primary transcription L generates uncapped antigenomic RNA molecules that are then capped using host cell-derived capped primers (cap snatching). L and S segment-transcribed mRNAs are translated by free ribosomes ( Garcin et al., 1995 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Meier et al., 2021 ). M segment-transcribed mRNA is translated by membrane-bound ribosomes, with the expressed GPC which is likely co-translationally cleaved by cellular proteases to yield G N and G C . The synthesis of the antigenome by L protein serves as a template for genomic RNA replication. Secondary transcription amplifies the synthesis of mRNAs and genome replication. During morphogenesis, G N and G C accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, modified host membranes are acquired, and virions bud into the Golgi. Biology Genus Orthohantavirus includes 38 species for 60 distinct viruses. These viruses and their unclassified, potential relatives, subclinically, and often chronically, infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla, and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents ( Jonsson et al., 2010 , Wu et al., 2018 , Chen et al., 2023 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are overall distributed worldwide, but the individual geographic distribution is dependent on host range. At least some orthohantaviruses may not be as restricted to a particular host as originally thought, but may be carried by animals of multiple hosts ( Goodfellow et al., 2021 , Quizon et al., 2022 , Gu et al., 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease (all in humans) and all disease-causing viruses are rodent-borne. Human infection may occur after inhalation of aerosolized excreta or secreta of infected rodents or direct rodent contact. The two WHO-recognized orthohantavirus-caused diseases are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Asian and European viruses (in particular Dobrava virus [DOBV], Hantaan virus [HTNV], Puumala virus [PUUV] and Seoul virus [SEOV]), and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a frequently lethal disease caused by viruses from the Americas (in particular Andes virus [ANDV] and Sin Nombre virus [SNV]) ( Vial et al., 2023 ). The hamster model of wild-type ANDV infection is lethal and largely mimics human HPS ( Hooper et al., 2001 ). After SNV infection in nonhuman primates, some animals develop an HPS-like disease, but cell passage of SNV can result in mutations that render the virus non-pathogenic in this model ( Safronetz et al., 2014 ). Many rodent models result in a chronic, asymptomatic infection, and these have been used in early-stage therapeutic studies ( Strandin et al., 2020 ). However, recent advances have been made in development of an HFRS mouse model using HTNV variants ( Wei et al., 2022 ). Orthohantavirus animal models are reviewed in ( Golden et al., 2015 ). Antigenicity There is considerable serum cross-reactivity between the nucleocapsids of hantavirids, but neutralizing antibodies targeting Gn/Gc are more specific. SNV was first identified as a hantavirid based on cross-reactivity of patient sera with other orthohantavirus antigens ( 1993 ). Similarly, rodents that carried SNV were identified in serosurveys using non-SNV orthohantavirus antigens, since SNV had not been isolated at the time ( Childs et al., 1994 ). Species demarcation criteria Demarcation of species is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Laenen et al., 2019 ). Phylogenetic relationships across the genus have been estimated using maximum likelihood trees generated from complete N, GPC and L amino-acid sequences, and for N and GPC amino-acid sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Hantaviridae ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Hantaviridae (taxid:1980413) VIRION Enveloped, spherical. Diameter from 80 to 120nm. GENOME Segmented Negative-stranded RNA linear genome, L segment is between 6.8 and 12 kb, M segment between 3.2 and 4.9 kb and S segment between 1 and 3 kb. Encodes for four to six proteins. Some hantaviruses also encode a NSs protein on their S segment. GENE EXPRESSION The viral RNA dependent RNA polymerase (L) binds to a promoter on each encapsidated segment, and transcribes the mRNA. These are capped by L protein during synthesis using cap snatching . Transcription is terminated by a strong hairpin sequence at the end of each gene. Puumala virus expressed an additional NSs by leaky scanning in the NS gene. ENZYMES RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L Cap Snatching endonuclease L REPLICATION CYTOPLASMIC Virus attaches to host receptors though Gn-Gc glycoprotein dimer, and is endocytosed into vesicles in the host cell. Fusion of virus membrane with the vesicle membrane; ribonucleocapsid segments are released in the cytoplasm. Transcription , viral mRNAs are capped in the cytoplasm. Replication presumably starts when enough nucleoprotein is present to encapsidate neo-synthetized antigenomes and genomes. The ribonucleocapsids buds at Golgi apparatus, releasing the virion by exocytosis. The hantaviruses (Hantaviridae) ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Back to Andes virus resource There are approximately 92 known viruses in the family Hantaviridae, classified into 52 species. Each species is typically adapted to a specific reservoir host, most commonly rodents, but also bats and moles. With the notable exception of Andes virus, hantaviruses are generally not transmitted from person to person. Based on their geographic distribution, evolutionary relationships, and the diseases they cause in humans, hantaviruses can be broadly divided into three major groups: New World hantaviruses (the Americas) These viruses cause Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a severe respiratory disease. Important examples include Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. Annual incidence are about 100 cases per year (Andes virus) about 25 cases per year (Sin Nombre virus) Old World hantaviruses (Asia) These viruses are responsible for Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. Major examples include Hantaan virus and Seoul virus. Annual incidence: more than 10,000 cases worldwide Old World hantaviruses (Europe) European hantaviruses typically cause a milder form of HFRS known as Nephropathia epidemica (NE). The main causative agents are Puumala virus and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Annual incidence: more than 1,000 cases Together, these viruses represent an important and diverse group of zoonotic pathogens that can cause severe disease following accidental transmission from their natural animal hosts to humans.

papers.title: Hantavirus preparedness at human-rodent interfaces: lessons from China's HFRS control and Andes virus transmission in mobile populations.
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are globally distributed reservoir-associated viruses that cause haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), mainly in Eurasia, and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS; also termed hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, HPS), mainly in the Americas. Most human infections arise from exposure to rodent-contaminated environments, so clustered disease may reflect shared environmental exposure rather than interpersonal transmission. This Review uses China's long-term HFRS experience as a central case study for interface-centred preparedness. China demonstrates that sustained surveillance, reservoir monitoring, risk-defined vaccination, rodent control and environmental risk reduction can substantially reduce disease burden, but declining incidence does not mean disappearance of ecological risk. Its dual HTNV and SEOV ecology further shows that one clinical syndrome can arise from distinct agricultural and peri-domestic rat-associated interfaces. Andes virus (ANDV) provides a contrasting challenge: selected outbreaks have documented limited but consequential human-to-human transmission after close or prolonged contact. The 2026 MV Hondius event illustrates how such transmission can become an international contact-tracing problem when it occurs in mobile populations. Preparedness should therefore combine long-term management of rodent-derived interfaces, rapid discrimination between common-source clusters and ANDV secondary transmission, and response systems that remain effective when exposed persons, infected animals or close contacts cross geographical borders.

full_text_sections.abstract: Hantaviruses are globally distributed reservoir-associated viruses that cause haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), mainly in Eurasia, and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS; also termed hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, HPS), mainly in the Americas. Most human infections arise from exposure to rodent-contaminated environments, so clustered disease may reflect shared environmental exposure rather than interpersonal transmission. This Review uses China's long-term HFRS experience as a central case study for interface-centred preparedness. China demonstrates that sustained surveillance, reservoir monitoring, risk-defined vaccination, rodent control and environmental risk reduction can substantially reduce disease burden, but declining incidence does not mean disappearance of ecological risk. Its dual HTNV and SEOV ecology further shows that one clinical syndrome can arise from distinct agricultural and peri-domestic rat-associated interfaces. Andes virus (ANDV) provides a contrasting challenge: selected outbreaks have documented limited but consequential human-to-human transmission after close or prolonged contact. The 2026 MV Hondius event illustrates how such transmission can become an international contact-tracing problem when it occurs in mobile populations. Preparedness should therefore combine long-term management of rodent-derived interfaces, rapid discrimination between common-source clusters and ANDV secondary transmission, and response systems that remain effective when exposed persons, infected animals or close contacts cross geographical borders.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause HFRS in Eurasia and HCPS/HPS in the Americas, with most human cases from rodent‑contaminated environments, prompting a review of preparedness at human‑rodent interfaces. Main directions: The review highlights China’s integrated surveillance, vaccination, rodent control, and environmental risk reduction, the dual HTNV/SEOV ecology across agricultural and peri‑domestic settings, the distinct challenge of Andes virus human‑to‑human spread in mobile populations, and the need for rapid discrimination of transmission modes. Current state: Evidence shows that sustained Chinese measures have markedly lowered HFRS burden while ecological risk remains, and that ANDV can transmit between humans but only after close, prolonged contact. papers.title: Immunopathogenesis of vascular leakage in hantavirus infections: a systematic review of mechanisms underlying HPS and HFRS
papers.abstract: Hantavirus infections manifest as Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS) and Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS), both associated with increased vascular permeability despite the lack of direct cytopathic injury to endothelial cells. A systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science (January 2020–May 2026) identified human studies investigating immunopathogenic mechanisms in HPS or HFRS. Due to substantial heterogeneity across study designs, findings were synthesized descriptively. Forty-one studies (39 cohorts, 2 case–control) were included, predominantly on HFRS-associated hantaviruses (HTNV, PUUV, DOBV); only one study evaluated HPS-associated ANDV. The reviewed literature revealed elevated inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-18, CXCL10, CX3CL1), depletion of Mucosal-Associated Invariant T (MAIT) cells linked to IRE1αdependent pyroptosis, disruption of the endothelial glycocalyx, and coagulation disturbances with platelet dysfunction. Biomarkers of glycocalyx injury (heparan sulfate, chondroitin sulfate, and soluble thrombomodulin) were associated with increased mortality risk (AUC 0.87–0.93). No human mechanistic studies on Sin Nombre virus (SNV) were identified. Hantavirus-induced vascular leakage is driven by cytokine-mediated endothelial dysfunction, MAIT cell pyroptosis, glycocalyx degradation, and immunothrombosis. While HFRS mechanisms are now well-characterized, the absence of human mechanistic data for HPS—particularly for SNV—remains a critical gap.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus infections cause HPS and HFRS with vascular leakage despite no direct endothelial injury. Main directions: Elevated cytokines, MAIT cell pyroptosis, glycocalyx loss, and coagulation disturbances are central mechanisms. Current state: These pathways drive leakage, and HFRS mechanisms are well‑characterized. Gaps: Human mechanistic data for HPS, especially SNV, are absent. Future research: Conduct human mechanistic studies on HPS and SNV to validate biomarkers and clarify pathogenic processes.

papers.title: Revisiting Animal Reservoirs of Hantavirus and Other Zoonotic Viruses Associated with Cruise Travel: Impact and Prevention
papers.abstract: The sustained growth of international maritime tourism and the expansion of the cruise industry have increased the importance of emerging zoonotic diseases as a significant challenge to global public health. Cruise ships constitute complex epidemiological settings characterized by high population density, rapid international mobility, and constant interaction between humans, animals, and coastal environments, factors that favor the introduction and spread of emerging infectious agents. Potential zoonotic concerns include orthohantaviruses and other zoonotic viruses, such as dengue, chikungunya, Zika, yellow fever, and avian influenza, which are associated with animal reservoirs and vectors in ports, tourist destinations, and tropical ecosystems. This review examines the ecology of animal reservoirs of orthohantaviruses and other zoonotic pathogens relevant to maritime tourism, including peri-urban rodents, bats, migratory birds, and other mammals. It discusses how climate change, coastal urbanization, and environmental change affect viral transmission dynamics. It highlights epidemiological risks linked to international cruises, particularly exposure during ecotourism excursions, pathogen introduction, and challenges for maritime surveillance. The review also addresses travel medicine, biosecurity, and infection control, emphasizing a One Health approach. Strengthening integrated surveillance and prevention systems is essential to ensure safer, more sustainable, and resilient maritime tourism in the 21st century.

papers.title: Differences in Ecological Drivers for Leptospira and Hantavirus in an Urban Norway Rat Population.
papers.abstract: Rodent control in urban areas is an important public health measure, among other reasons, for their capacity of harboring several zoonotic pathogens. Efficient, evidence-based control programs must consider both rodent and pathogen ecology, to achieve both rodent population and pathogen transmission risk reduction. The present study aims to determine the ecological drivers of Leptospira and Hantavirus positivity in an urban Norway Rat population. One hundred and twenty rats were trapped in four urban poor communities in Salvador, Brazil, tested for Leptospira sp. and Hantavirus. Generalized Linear Models for Leptospira (N=109) and Hantavirus (N=108) positivity were created with a pool of environmental and demographic variables, followed by stepwise model selection using Akaike's Information Criterion. Age, presence of Calodium hepaticum scars, wounds, accumulated materials, open sewer canals and unpaved soil were positively associated with Leptospira positivity. Age and presence of accumulated materials were positively associated with Hantavirus positivity, while rodent control campaigns and being male were protective factors. Factors associated with positivity for Leptospira are also associated with rodent infestation. Different subsets of environmental and demographic factors influence pathogens with different epidemiological characteristics. Control measures that effectively reduce zoonotic risk must consider the ecological characteristics of the pathogens present in the system.
authors: Ana Maria Borges da Paixão Barreto

Efficient, evidence-based control programs must consider both rodent and pathogen ecology, to achieve both rodent population and pathogen transmission risk reduction. The present study aims to determine the ecological drivers of Leptospira and Hantavirus positivity in an urban Norway Rat population. One hundred and twenty rats were trapped in four urban poor communities in Salvador, Brazil, tested for Leptospira sp. and Hantavirus. Generalized Linear Models for Leptospira (N=109) and Hantavirus (N=108) positivity were created with a pool of environmental and demographic variables, followed by stepwise model selection using Akaike's Information Criterion. Age, presence of Calodium hepaticum scars, wounds, accumulated materials, open sewer canals and unpaved soil were positively associated with Leptospira positivity. Age and presence of accumulated materials were positively associated with Hantavirus positivity, while rodent control campaigns and being male were protective factors. Factors associated with positivity for Leptospira are also associated with rodent infestation. Different subsets of environmental and demographic factors influence pathogens with different epidemiological characteristics. Control measures that effectively reduce zoonotic risk must consider the ecological characteristics of the pathogens present in the system.

Similar content being viewed by others Introduction Old world rats (genus Rattus) are the most ubiquitous synanthropic animals. Their global distribution and occurrence arise from their intimate relationship with human presence, following major human movements throughout the globe, such as the Transatlantic navigation and the Silk Route (Morand et al. 2015). Currently, rats are almost exclusively associated with human occupation, often of urbanized areas, are significantly dependent on the resources made available by human activity (Feng and Himsworth 2013). The relationship between rats and humans is not harmonious, with rats being considered pests, causing damage to farming and infrastructure, and contaminating food stocks (Jacob and Buckle 2018). Estimations suggest, conservatively, that the Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus, alone causes economic damage of more than USD 30 million/year globally (Diagne et al. 2023). Throughout the Global South, the fast growth of urban centers often results in the creation of informal settlements, characterized by deficiencies in the provision and coverage of basic urban services (e.g., trash collection, sanitation, pest control) and infrastructure (Carvalho-Pereira et al. 2024; Costa et al. 2014; de Oliveira et al. 2024). The resulting environment is highly conductive to rodent infestation, with an abundance of water, food and shelter (Panti-May et al. 2016). Such close coexistence exposes the populations of the settlements to the pathogens carried by rats (Costa, Ribeiro, et al. 2014; Muschetto et al. 2025). The role of rats as a zoonotic pathogen reservoir is arguably one of the most impactful threats posed by our proximity. Rodents host a remarkable diversity of zoonotic pathogens, including viruses, bacteria, unicellular eukaryote and helminth parasites (Luis et al. 2013; Himsworth et al. 2013; Delaney, Treuting, and Rothenburger 2018). Some of the most historically relevant pathogens have rodents as their reservoir, such as Yersinia pestis (Rahelinirina et al. 2021), Leptospira sp. (A. Minter et al. 2017) and Hantavirus (Dearing and Dizney 2010). Depending on the pathogen, rodents can either be direct sources of infection or act as part of the transmission cycle, shedding bacteria to the environment or promoting infective contact with competent hosts that thus infect humans (Himsworth et al. 2013). Important examples of pathogens carried by Norway rats are Leptospira spp. (Feng and Himsworth 2013), Hantavirus (Chen et al. 2023), and Toxoplasma gondii (Bazan et al. 2025). Leptospira spp., the causative agent of leptospirosis, is a genus of bacteria transmitted by water and soil contaminated by the urine of infected hosts such as rats, which are asymptomatic carriers and chronic shedders of the bacteria (Guerra 2009; Tucunduva de Faria et al. 2007). With over one million estimated human cases per year (Costa et al. 2015), the infection can cause asymptomatic/mild forms or evolve into severe and potentially lethal forms such as Weil’s disease and Leptospirosis-associated pulmonary hemorrhage syndrome (Ko, Goarant, and Picardeau 2009). In Salvador, leptospirosis is a long-standing challenge to public health in impoverished urban communities (Ko et al. 1999; Ribeiro et al. 2008). Hantavirus (Hantaviridae: genus Orthohantavirus) is a genus of negative-sense RNA viruses maintained mainly by small mammals (Bradfute et al. 2024), with several species pathogenic to humans. The clade is divided in Old World Hantaviruses (e.g., Orthohantavirus seoulense [SEOV], Orthohantavirus hantanense [HTNV]), causative agents of Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome, and New World Hantaviruses (e.g., Orthohantavirus andense [ANDV], Orthohantavirus sinnombreense [SNV]), causative agents of Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (Chen et al. 2023). Norway rats are the main reservoirs of Orthohantavirus seoulense, with chronic, nearly asymptomatic infection (Jonsson et al.2010; Meyer and Schmaljohn 2000). SEOV is considered to be cosmopolitan following the worldwide distribution of rats (Himsworth et al. 2013) and has been previously detected in rats in Salvador (Costa et al. 2014). Toxoplasma gondii is an apicomplexan parasite that widely infects warm-blooded animals, causing grave illness in immunocompromised individuals, as well as fetal development issues through congenital toxoplasmosis (S.G. Sanchez and Besteiro 2021). While important for the epidemiology of toxoplasmosis, infection by T. gondii in rats causes behavioral changes, but limited health effects (Ruffolo et al. 2016; Webster 1994). For the control of rat-borne zoonoses, the ecology of the zoonotic system should also be considered, as this presents its own ecological characteristics (Caio et al. 2016), an important consideration given the diversity of pathogens that rats can carry, including potential coinfections (Carvalho-Pereira et al. 2018; Costa et al. 2014; L.K.F. Lee et al. 2023). Previous studies in urban informal settlements in Salvador have investigated urban rodent ecology (Panti-May et al. 2016; C. G. Zeppelini et al. 2021; Eyre et al. 2020), movement (Awoniyi et al. 2021), the parasites and pathogens they carry (Costa, Porter, et al. 2014; Carvalho-Pereira et al. 2018), and the impacts of infestation on human health (Costa, Ribeiro, et al. 2014; Costa et al. 2021). However, studies have focused on isolated pathogens (Souza et al. 2021; Bazan et al. 2025; Pimentel Sobrinho et al. 2020), not yet evaluating potential ecological interactions between these pathogens, such as how environmental and demographic factors might differ between them. Knowledge of pathogen ecology of Norway rats, a multi-pathogen reservoir, including prevalence and pathogen characteristics and the impacts of environmental factors on their dynamics is essential to lead to targeted control and intervention strategies. Different pathogens can present different characteristics (e.g., acquisition route, tissue tropism, requirements for transmission) even if infecting the same host species, likely resulting in different responses to control measures. Our study aims to quantify zoonotic positivity for three different pathogens (Hantavirus, Leptospira spp. and Toxoplasma gondii) in Norway rats from urban impoverished communities in the city of Salvador, Bahia, Brazil, and identify whether the ecological processes that drive rat infection risk vary between pathogens. Characterizing zoonotic spillover risk in rodents and identifying environmental risk factors is fundamental for the development of rodent-borne zoonosis control programs that are resilient against the risk of pathogen (re)emergence as an unpredicted negative effect of the control program itself. Materials and Methods Ethical Statement Rodent sampling and biological sample harvesting procedures were authorized under license from the Ethics Committee for Animal Use of Fiocruz Bahia (authorization #019/2016). The study was conducted and reported following ARRIVE guidelines. Study Site The city of Salvador, Bahia (12° 55′ 28.03" S, 38° 28′ 34.9′′ W) is one of the largest urban centers in Brazil, with 692,819 km2 and over 2.5 million inhabitants, 42.7% of which living in informal settlements (henceforth communities) (IBGE 2022, 2015). Four communities were sampled: Marechal Rondon (MR), Alto do Cabrito (AC), Rio Sena (RS) e Nova Constituinte (NC), selected for their location in the same sanitary district (subdivisions of the city’s territory used for the operations of health authorities, including the Zoonosis Control Center [CCZ]), reflecting their sociodemographic similarity and environmental profile, which fit the criteria for classification as slums (inadequate housing conditions, limited or absent access to safe drinking water and sanitation), (Economic and Affairs 2019), and lack of adequate solid waste collection (including formation of open trash piles). All four communities were set on hills, with small natural waterways running at their lowermost point, which receive the communities’ household sewage. According to the CCZ, the communities have chronic issues with rodent infestation. In each community, the study area was defined as a polygon of 0.07–0.09 km2. Zoonotic Positivity for Rattus Norvegicus Rat capture data, and environmental and biological samples (kidney imprints, urine, blood and brain matter) were obtained from a previous field sampling study conducted in four communities, performed in two campaigns (40 semi-randomized trapping points with two Tomahawk-type traps, 4 trap-nights per campaign, April-June and October–November 2018) (C. G. Zeppelini et al. 2021). During necropsy and tissue sample harvesting, the presence of Calodium hepaticum (a helminth species that parasitises the liver of mammals, frequently observed in wild Rattus) was registered during the examination of the liver. The presence of the characteristic scars in the liver cortex was considered as a positive detection for the individual (Fuehrer 2014). Positivity for Leptospira was assessed by a combination of Indirect Fluorescent Antibody (IFA) assays performed on Poli-L-Lysine-treated microscope slides with kidney imprints (D et al. 2016) and/or urine sample qPCR targeting the lipL32 gene as previously described (Costa, Wunder, et al. 2015). Hantavirus positivity was determined by Enzyme-linked Immunoassay (ELISA) tests, using orthohantavirus purified recombinant nucleoprotein as antigen (Padula et al. 2000). Detection of Toxoplasma was performed through nested-PCR tests targeting the IST1 region of T. gondii (Hurtado et al. 2001). Due to limitations in availability, PCR tests for Hantavirus (RT-PCR targeting the Hantavirus-specific RNA-dependent RNA polymerase-encoding L segment) were restricted to ELISA-positive rats. All PCR tests were negative. The physical condition of rats was measured as a weight-length ratio that took into account the effect of age (Peig and Green 2009). Age of individuals was calculated in days based in morphometric data following the von Bertalanffy equation, with parameters obtained by fitting data derived from the growth curve for male rats (Calhoun 1962; Burthe et al. 2009). Morphology data, presence of parasites and of wounds were obtained during animal processing (C. G. Zeppelini et al. 2021). Environmental Variables A standardized descriptive questionnaire was applied to obtain the environmental data used to characterize the environment at each sampling point. The data collection occurred at the moment of trapping, being performed considering a 20-m-radius buffer around the sampling point (C. G. Zeppelini et al. 2021). Variables describe the presence of other animals, human-made materials (refuse, construction materials, debris), soil condition and presence of water, as well as rodent control activities (both carried by the locals themselves and by the Zoonosis Control Center) in the region at the moment the traps were set. Data on opossum presence were derived from captures during the trapping period. Data on presence of animals and rodent control measures in the trapping area (i.e., household backyards) were voluntarily provided by the resident during trap setting. Variables collected are listed in Table 1. Statistical Analysis To evaluate each outcome (positivity for Leptospira, Toxoplasma, or Hantavirus), a set of variables was defined based on hypotheses that link the biological processes known to be relevant to each pathogen to the outcome (Table 1). Positivity for the other pathogens was also added as a variable to evaluate if coinfection affects the chances of positivity for each zoonotic pathogen. Collinearity was verified through the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF), with variables having a VIF under 5 considered apt to compose the variable pool for each outcome. Generalized linear models (GLMs) were performed for each outcome using the VIF-verified and hypothesis-associated variables, followed by backwards stepwise model selection based on the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC). Models were considered plausible when ΔAIC < 2 compared to the model with the lowest AIC and selected based on maximum parsimony (lowest ΔAIC and number of variables). All analyses were performed using the packages Tidyverse, lme4 e MuMIn, on R Core Team, 2026 (Wickham et al. 2019; Bates et al. 2015; Barton 2022). Results Zoonotic Positivity for Rattus Norvegicus One-hundred and sixteen individuals were tested for Leptospira, with 48.3% positivity (56/116); 117 tested for Hantavirus with 31.6% positivity (37/117) and 9 samples with indeterminate status; and 120 tested for Toxoplasma, with 2.5% positivity (3/120). Due to the low positivity for Toxoplasma, only Hantavirus and Leptospira were analysed by GLM and model selection. The model for Leptospira was performed with 109 individuals (7 individuals removed due to incomplete associated data), with this subset presenting 48.6% (53/109) positivity, and 108 individuals were employed for the Hantavirus model (9 individuals removed due to incomplete data), presenting 33.3% (36/108) positivity. From the subsets with complete data, 39.6% (21/53) of the Leptospira-positive rats were also positive for Hantavirus, while 58.3% (21/36) of orthohantavirus-positive rats were also positive for Leptospira. Leptospira Positivity Model Fifty-six models were considered plausible (ΔAIC <2) after model selection. Among the plausible models, five were equally parsimonious (four variables each), containing six variables between them. These six variables were age estimated in days (present in 49/56 plausible models), presence of Calodium hepaticum scars in the liver (50/56), presence of open sewers within a 20-m-radius buffer (37/56), the presence of accumulated materials (45/56), type of ground cover (54/56), and presence of wounds (56/56) (for the full model selection table, see Appendix S1: Table S1). Age in days (OR 1.02 [1–1.04], p=0.083), presence of C. hepaticum scars in the liver (OR 2.41 [0.9–6.3], p=0.084), presence of accumulated materials (OR 3.2 [0.82–14.9], p=0.109), presence of open sewers within the 20 m buffer (OR 2.03 [0.82–5.19], p=0.13), the presence of unpaved soil (OR 2.75 [1.06–7.46], p=0.041), and the presence of wounds (OR 7.62 [1.15–153.94], p=0.075) all increased the odds of positivity (Table 2). Hantavirus positivity model Forty models were considered plausible (ΔAIC<2) according to the results of model selection (for the full model selection table, see Appendix S1: Table S2). The single most parsimonious model contained four variables, namely sex (present in 40/40 plausible models), age in days (40/40), Centre for the Control of Zoonoses (CCZ) activity (38/40) and presence of accumulated materials (40/40). According to the model, CCZ activity (OR 0.32 [0.12–0.83] p=0.022) and being a male (OR 0.25 [0.08–0.66], p=0.007) reduced the odds of positivity. In contrast, age (OR 1.05 [1.02–1.07], p<0.001) and presence of accumulated materials (OR 12.42 [2.25–113.25], p=0.01) increased the odds of positivity (Table 2). Discussion Our results support the hypothesis that different pathogens are associated with different ecological variables. Only two variables analyzed were common to both pathogens – age (in days) and the presence of accumulated materials (all non-garbage items accumulated in the environment, including but not limited to piles of construction materials, construction debris and large discarded items). Infections by Leptospira were associated with environmental factors, particularly anthropogenic modifications, relevant to the environmental component of the pathogen’s transmission, namely the presence of sewage and unpaved, pervious soil (A. Minter et al. 2017), as well as with coinfection with another parasite, the nematode Calodium hepaticum. Infections by Hantavirus were associated with rodent control carried by CCZ, considered a demographic stressor (C. G. Zeppelini et al. 2021). The ubiquitous presence of factors associated with environmental vulnerability and absence of necessary management highlights the importance of environmental health as a pillar of the One Health framework and opportunities for evidence-based management and control (Gittleman 2024). The age of individuals increased the chances of positivity for both pathogens. analysis.background: Rodent control in urban areas is important for public health because rats harbor multiple zoonotic pathogens, and effective programs must consider both rodent and pathogen ecology. This study aimed to identify ecological drivers of Leptospira and Hantavirus positivity in an urban Norway rat population.
analysis.methods: One hundred and twenty Norway rats were trapped in four urban poor communities in Salvador, Brazil, and tested for Leptospira spp.; 109 rats were included in the Leptospira model and 108 in the Hantavirus model. Generalized Linear Models with environmental and demographic variables were built and reduced by stepwise Akaike’s Information Criterion selection.
analysis.results: Leptospira positivity was positively associated with age, Calodium hepaticum scars, wounds, accumulated materials, open sewer canals, and unpaved soil. Hantavirus positivity was positively associated with age and accumulated materials, while rodent control campaigns and male sex were protective.
analysis.contribution: Factors linked to Leptospira also relate to rodent infestation, indicating overlapping risk drivers. Distinct environmental and demographic subsets influence pathogens with different epidemiology, suggesting control measures must be pathogen‑specific.
analysis.limitations: No limitations are reported in the supplied evidence; the abstract provides limited methodological detail.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Rodent control is vital because rats carry many zoonoses, and this study sought ecological drivers of Leptospira and Hantavirus in urban Norway rats. Methods: 120 rats from four poor communities in Salvador, Brazil were sampled; 109 and 108 were used in GLMs for Leptospira and Hantavirus, respectively, with stepwise AIC selection of environmental and demographic variables. Results: Leptospira positivity correlated with age, Calodium hepaticum scars, wounds, accumulated material, open sewers, and unpaved soil; Hantavirus positivity correlated with age and accumulated material, while control campaigns and male sex were protective. Contribution: Overlapping drivers link Leptospira to rodent infestation, but each pathogen is shaped by distinct factor subsets, implying pathogen‑specific control. papers.title_zh: 城市挪威鼠群体中钩端螺旋体与 汉坦病毒 的生态驱动因素差异。

analysis_zh.background: 城市地区的鼠类控制对公共健康至关重要,因为老鼠携带多种人畜共患病原体,且有效的项目必须同时考虑鼠类和病原体的生态。本研究旨在识别城市挪威鼠群体中钩端螺旋体和 汉坦病毒 阳性的生态驱动因素。
analysis_zh.methods: 在巴西萨尔瓦多的四个城市贫困社区捕获了120只挪威鼠,并检测其钩端螺旋体 spp.;其中109只纳入钩端螺旋体模型,108只纳入 汉坦病毒 模型。构建了包含环境和人口学变量的广义线性模型,并通过逐步AIC(赤池信息准则)选择进行模型简化。
analysis_zh.results: 钩端螺旋体阳性与年龄、肝吸虫瘢痕、伤口、堆积物、开放式下水道渠和未铺设土壤呈正相关。汉坦病毒 阳性与年龄和堆积物呈正相关,而鼠类控制行动和雄性则具有保护作用。
analysis_zh.contribution: 与钩端螺旋体相关的因素亦与鼠类侵扰相关,表明风险驱动因素存在重叠。不同的环境和人口学子集影响流行病学不同的病原体,提示控制措施需针对特定病原体制定。
analysis_zh.limitations: 提供的证据中未报告任何局限性;摘要仅提供了有限的方法学细节。

papers.title: Hantavirus RNA Detection in Small Mammals and Spatial Association with Human Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome in the West Kazakhstan Region, 2025
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a zoonotic disease associated with orthohantaviruses maintained in natural rodent hosts. This study assessed the detection and spatial distribution of hantavirus RNA among small mammals in the West Kazakhstan Region in 2025 and compared rodent surveillance findings with human HFRS occurrence. An observational descriptive-analytical study was conducted in August–September 2025 in four districts. A total of 343 small mammals were captured and morphologically identified. Lung tissues were tested using 123 pooled testing units, while 14 specimens were tested individually during the same surveillance campaign. Thus, 137 testing units representing 343 animals were evaluated by real-time and conventional RT-PCR. The minimum infection rate (MIR) was calculated as a descriptive minimum estimate, and a pooled-testing likelihood model was used to account for variation in testing-unit size. Hantavirus RNA was detected in 47/137 testing units, including 45 positive pooled units and two individually positive specimens, corresponding to a descriptive MIR of 13.7%. The model-based individual-level infection probability was estimated at 18.0% (95% profile-likelihood CI: 13.5–23.1%). Positive testing units were observed among Apodemus uralensis, Myodes glareolus, and Microtus arvalis. At the district level, the descriptive MIR ranged from 11.6% in Burlinsky to 19.0% in Chingirlauisky. Sampling sites overlapped spatially with settlements reporting human HFRS cases, including Utvinka, Daryinsk, and Rubezhinskoye; however, spatial coincidence does not establish direct transmission.

An observational descriptive-analytical study was conducted in August–September 2025 in four districts. A total of 343 small mammals were captured and morphologically identified. Lung tissues were tested using 123 pooled testing units, while 14 specimens were tested individually during the same surveillance campaign. Thus, 137 testing units representing 343 animals were evaluated by real-time and conventional RT-PCR. The minimum infection rate (MIR) was calculated as a descriptive minimum estimate, and a pooled-testing likelihood model was used to account for variation in testing-unit size. Hantavirus RNA was detected in 47/137 testing units, including 45 positive pooled units and two individually positive specimens, corresponding to a descriptive MIR of 13.7%. The model-based individual-level infection probability was estimated at 18.0% (95% profile-likelihood CI: 13.5–23.1%). Positive testing units were observed among Apodemus uralensis, Myodes glareolus, and Microtus arvalis. At the district level, the descriptive MIR ranged from 11.6% in Burlinsky to 19.0% in Chingirlauisky. Sampling sites overlapped spatially with settlements reporting human HFRS cases, including Utvinka, Daryinsk, and Rubezhinskoye; however, spatial coincidence does not establish direct transmission.

analysis.background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a zoonotic disease linked to orthohantaviruses maintained in rodent hosts (A1).
analysis.methods: In August–September 2025, an observational descriptive‑analytical study captured 343 small mammals in four districts of West Kazakhstan, identified them morphologically, and tested lung tissue using 123 pooled and 14 individual RT‑PCR units (total 137 testing units) (A2, A3, A4, A5, A6).
analysis.results: Hantavirus RNA was detected in 47 of 137 testing units (descriptive MIR 13.7%); a pooled‑testing model estimated individual infection probability at 18.0% (95 % CI 13.5–23.1%) (A8, A9). Positive units were found in Apodemus uralensis, Myodes glareolus, and Microtus arvalis, with district MIR ranging from 11.6% to 19.0% (A10, A11).
analysis.contribution: The work maps rodent hantavirus prevalence and shows spatial overlap between infected rodent sites and human HFRS settlements, informing surveillance and risk assessment (A12, A13).
analysis.limitations: Only abstract data are available; spatial coincidence does not establish direct transmission, and detailed ecological or temporal analyses are not reported (A13).

analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS is a zoonotic disease associated with orthohantaviruses in rodent hosts. Methods: In Aug‑Sep 2025, an observational descriptive‑analytical study captured 343 small mammals in four West Kazakhstan districts and tested lung tissue via 137 pooled/individual RT‑PCR units. Results: Hantavirus RNA was found in 47/137 units (MIR 13.7%); model‑based infection probability was 18.0% (95 % CI 13.5–23.1%). Positive rodents included Apodemus uralensis, Myodes glareolus, and Microtus arvalis, with district MIR 11.6–19.0%. Contribution: The study maps rodent infection and its spatial overlap with human HFRS cases, aiding surveillance. Limitations: Only abstract information is provided; spatial overlap does not prove direct transmission.

papers.title: Hantaviruses at an inflection point: scientific evidence, spillover risk, and One Health approach
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are zoonotic RNA viruses that cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome and are primarily maintained in rodent reservoirs. Transmission to humans occurs mainly by inhalation of aerosolized excreta from infected rodents, but Andes virus uniquely shows documented limited person-to-person spread with important clinical and public-health implications. Environmental change, urbanization, and global mobility have broadened hantavirus geographic risk and contributed to recent multi-country clusters, including expedition cruise-ship–associated events that highlighted preparedness gaps. This review synthesizes current knowledge on hantavirus taxonomy, molecular biology, transmission pathways, host reservoirs, pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnostics, and management, and it critically assesses advances in molecular surveillance, phylogenetics, antiviral research, and emerging nanobiotechnological approaches. I operationalize a One Health framework into concrete prevention and control actions, integrated human–animal–environment surveillance, targeted rodent reservoir monitoring and control, environmental sampling, and formal intersectoral coordination mechanisms, and I map epidemiologic findings to prioritized, group-specific public-health interventions. Finally, I identify current controversies and knowledge gaps (reservoir competence, surveillance sensitivity, and limits of predictive models), and propose a research and policy agenda to strengthen global preparedness for high-consequence hantavirus events.

papers.full_text: Hantaviruses at an inflection point: scientific evidence, spillover risk, and One Health approach Ilyes Zatla * Independent Researcher, Tlemcen, Algeria Hantaviruses are zoonotic RNA viruses that cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome and are primarily main- tained in rodent reservoirs. Transmission to humans occurs mainly by inhalation of aerosolized excreta from infected rodents, but Andes virus uniquely shows documented limited person-to-person spread with important clinical and public- health implications. Environmental change, urbanization, and global mobility have broadened hantavirus geographic risk and contributed to recent multi-country clusters, including expedition cruise-ship–associated events that highlighted preparedness gaps. This review synthesizes current knowledge on hantavirus taxonomy, molecular biology, transmission pathways, host reservoirs, pathogen- esis, clinical features, diagnostics, and management, and it critically assesses advances in molecular surveillance, phylogenetics, antiviral research, and emerg- ing nanobiotechnological approaches. I operationalize a One Health framework into concrete prevention and control actions, integrated human–animal–envi- ronment surveillance, targeted rodent reservoir monitoring and control, environ- mental sampling, and formal intersectoral coordination mechanisms, and I map epidemiologic findings to prioritized, group-specific public-health interventions. Finally, I identify current controversies and knowledge gaps (reservoir compe- tence, surveillance sensitivity, and limits of predictive models), and propose a research and policy agenda to strengthen global preparedness for high-conse- quence hantavirus events. KEYWORDS disease transmission, epidemiology, Hantavirus, one health, physiopathology, therapeutics, zoonosis Introduction Hantaviruses are zoonotic pathogens that represent one of the most significant rodent- borne viral threats to human health. They are distributed worldwide and are associated with two major clinical syndromes: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), predom- inantly observed in Europe and Asia, and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), mainly reported in the Americas. These diseases differ in clinical presentation and mortality but share common virological and ecological characteristics (1, 2). The discovery of hantaviruses dates back to the Korean War during the early 1950s, when thousands of United Nations soldiers developed a severe febrile illness later identified as Korean hemorrhagic fever. The causative agent, Hantaan virus, was isolated in 1978 near Frontiers in Virology frontiersin.org 01 OPEN ACCESS EDITED BY Masako Nomaguchi, Tokushima University, Japan REVIEWED BY Kalimuthu Karuppanan, Sai University, India Jessenia Sabrina Navas Castillo, Hospital Roosevelt, Guatemala *CORRESPONDENCE Ilyes Zatla ilyes.zatla@aol.com RECEIVED 16 May 2026 REVISED 05 August 2026 ACCEPTED 05 August 2026 PUBLISHED 18 September 2026 CITATION Zatla I (2026) Hantaviruses at an inflection point: scientific evidence, spillover risk, and One Health approach. TYPE Review PUBLISHED 18 September 2026 DOI 10.3389/fviro.2026.1883348 the Hantan River in South Korea, giving rise to the name “hanta- virus.” Since then, numerous hantavirus species have been identi- fied globally, each associated with a specific rodent or small mammal reservoir. The global importance of hantaviruses has increased substan- tially during the last two decades. Ecological disturbances, defores- tation, climate fluctuations, agricultural expansion, and increasing human encroachment into wildlife habitats have enhanced oppor- tunities for rodent-human interactions. Concurrently, improved molecular surveillance has revealed previously unrecognized han- tavirus diversity and geographic expansion (3–5). Recent outbreaks linked to Andes virus in South America and a multi-country cruise ship-associated cluster in 2026 have once again highlighted the epidemic potential of hantaviruses and the importance of international preparedness (6–8). This narrative review was conducted through a comprehensive search of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, WHO reports, CDC resources, ECDC reports, and official public health documents published up to May 2026. Search terms included “hantavirus”, “orthohantavirus”, “HFRS”, “HCPS”, “Andes virus”, “Dobrava-Belgrade virus”, “zoonotic transmission”, “rodent reser- voirs”, “viral evolution”, “diagnosis”, “treatment”, “vaccines”, and “One Health”. Priority was given to peer-reviewed articles, system- atic reviews, surveillance reports, and official outbreak communi- cations. Studies lacking scientific validation, duplicate reports, and non-relevant publications were excluded. Epidemiology and global distribution of hantaviruses Hantaviruses demonstrate a wide but geographically structured global distribution, with distinct viral species and associated clinical syndromes predominating in different regions. The epidemiology is largely shaped by the distribution of rodent reservoirs, environmental conditions, and human exposure patterns. Two major clinical syndromes define the global burden of disease: HFRS, predominantly seen in Eurasia, and HCPS, mainly reported in the Americas (9, 10). In Asia, China represents the country with the highest global burden of HFRS, accounting for thousands of reported cases annually. The disease remains endemic in multiple provinces, largely driven by rodent species such as Apodemus agrarius and Rattus norvegicus, which serve as natural reservoirs. South Korea and parts of the Russian Federation also remain important endemic zones, where seasonal outbreaks are frequently reported, often associated with agricultural activities and increased human– rodent contact in rural environments (11). In Europe, hantavirus infections are primarily caused by Puumala virus, which is responsible for a milder form of HFRS known as nephropathia epidemica. This virus is widely distributed across Northern and Central Europe, with recurrent outbreaks documented in countries such as Finland, Sweden, Germany, and France. These outbreaks are often cyclical and strongly influenced by ecological factors, particularly fluctuations in bank vole populations (Myodes glareolus), which serve as the principal reservoir (12–17). In south- eastern Europe, Bulgaria represents an important endemic area for hantavirus infections, particularly those associated with Dobrava– Belgrade virus (DOBV). Molecular and epidemiological studies have demonstrated circulation of hantaviruses in both human patients and rodent reservoirs, emphasizing their continued public health rele- vance in the region (18–21). In the Americas, hantavirus infections manifest predominantly as HCPS, a severe respiratory disease associated with high case- fatality rates. Reported cases are concentrated in North, Central, and South America, with significant disease burden in the United States, Argentina, Chile, Brazil, and Paraguay. Among the circulat- ing species, Andes virus is of particular epidemiological concern due to its unique ability to transmit between humans under specific conditions, a feature not commonly observed in most other hantaviruses. This characteristic has contributed to notable out- breaks in South America and remains a focal point of public health surveillance (22). These epidemiological observations have direct implications for prevention. Regions experiencing increased rodent abundance following climatic events should strengthen rodent surveillance, reinforce public education, and enhance clinical awareness during seasonal peaks. Likewise, international travel- associated clusters highlight the need for cross-border surveillance and rapid case notification. Despite considerable advances in global surveillance, the true epidemiological burden of hantavirus infections remains uncertain. Underdiagnosis is likely substantial, particularly in Africa and many low- and middle-income countries, where limited diagnostic ca- pacity, inadequate surveillance systems, and overlap with other febrile illnesses may obscure disease recognition. Moreover, sur- veillance methodologies vary considerably between countries, lim- iting the comparability of incidence estimates and hindering the establishment of standardized global risk assessments. Another major challenge concerns the impact of climate change on hanta- virus emergence. Although ecological studies suggest that changing temperature, precipitation patterns, and land-use modifications influence rodent population dynamics and spillover risk, the magnitude and consistency of these associations remain incom- pletely understood. Future epidemiological research should prior- itize harmonized surveillance protocols, expanded genomic surveillance, and long-term ecological studies integrating climatic, environmental, and epidemiological data to improve outbreak prediction and preparedness. Current outbreaks and public health concerns Recent epidemiological observations highlight ongoing con- cerns regarding hantavirus emergence and re-emergence in multi- ple regions. WHO-reported clusters have raised attention toward potential multi-country exposure events, including those associated with international travel, where suspected Andes virus infections have been investigated in the context of severe respiratory illness Zatla 10.3389/fviro.2026.1883348 Frontiers in Virology frontiersin.org 02 and fatal outcomes. Although such reports remain under investi- gation, they emphasize the importance of global surveillance in detecting cross-border transmission events (8). In parallel, an increasing number of hantavirus cases has been reported in Argentina during the 2025–2026 period; however, the factors contributing to this trend remain under investigation. These trends have been discussed in the context of broader ecological and climatic shifts that may influence rodent population dynamics and human exposure risk (23, 24). Factors such as deforestation, agricultural expansion, urban encroachment into wildlife habitats, and climate variability are considered key drivers that may facilitate future spillover events. Despite public and media concern, current scientific evidence consistently indicates that hantaviruses do not possess efficient airborne transmission capabilities comparable to respiratory viruses such as influenza or SARS-CoV-2. Human-to-human transmission remains rare and is largely restricted to specific strains, most notably Andes virus, and typically requires prolonged close contact. This epidemiological constraint is a critical factor limiting wide- spread global dissemination (25–27). Public health surveillance and One Health perspectives Effective control and prevention of hantavirus infections require an integrated One Health approach that acknowledges the intercon- nectedness of human, animal, and environmental health (Figure 1). Surveillance strategies must simultaneously target human clinical cases, rodent reservoir populations, and environmental conditions that influence viral maintenance and spillover risk. Modern public health frameworks increasingly incorporate wildlife monitoring systems to track reservoir abundance and viral prevalence, alongside environmental management strategies aimed at reducing human exposure. In addition, genomic surveil- lance has become a powerful tool for understanding viral evolution, transmission pathways, and phylogeographic patterns, enabling more precise outbreak reconstruction and risk assessment (28). Advances in molecular epidemiology, particularly high- throughput sequencing technologies, have significantly improved the ability to detect viral variants and trace interregional spread. When combined with climate modeling and ecological forecasting, these approaches allow for more predictive and proactive outbreak preparedness strategies (29). Ultimately, addressing hantavirus threats requires sustained interdisciplinary collaboration among virologists, epidemiologists, ecologists, clinicians, and public health authorities. Such coordina- tion is essential to strengthen early warning systems, improve outbreak response capacity, and mitigate the impact of future zoonotic emergence events. Taxonomy and classification of hantaviruses Hantaviruses are classified within the order Bunyavirales and the family Hantaviridae, representing a distinct lineage of enveloped, negative-sense single-stranded RNA viruses. Historically, hantaviruses FIGURE 1 One Health framework for hantavirus emergence, prevention and outbreak preparedness. Zatla 10.3389/fviro.2026.1883348 Frontiers in Virology frontiersin.org 03 were grouped within the broader family Bunyaviridae; however, advances in molecular phylogenetics, genome sequencing, and evolu- tionary analysis have led to a major taxonomic revision. This restructuring resulted in the establishment of Hantaviridae as a separate family, reflecting the unique genetic and biological charac- teristics of hantaviruses compared to other bunyaviruses (30, 31). Within this family, the genus Orthohantavirus includes the majority of species that are pathogenic to humans. Members of this genus are responsible for the two principal clinical syndromes associated with hantavirus infection: HFRS and HCPS. Several medically significant species have been identified, including Hantaan virus (HTNV), Seoul virus (SEOV), Puumala virus (PUUV), Dobrava–Belgrade virus (DOBV), Sin Nombre virus (SNV), and Andes virus (ANDV). These viruses differ in their geographic distribution, clinical severity, and epidemiological behavior, but share common structural and genomic features characteristic of the genus (30–33). A defining feature of hantavirus biology is the strong associa- tion between each viral species and a specific rodent reservoir host. This host specificity reflects a long evolutionary history of virus– host coevolution, resulting in highly adapted and often asymptom- atic infections in natural rodent populations. The maintenance of hantaviruses in nature is therefore primarily dependent on persis- tent infection within these reservoir species, with human infection occurring as an incidental spillover event rather than as part of the natural transmission cycle. This ecological and evolutionary rela- tionship is central to understanding hantavirus emergence and persistence across different geographic regions.(30, 34) Viral structure and genome organization Hantaviruses are enveloped, spherical virions typically measur- ing approximately 80–120 nm in diameter. Their structural orga- nization is characteristic of members of the family Hantaviridae, with a lipid envelope derived from the host cell membrane. Embedded within this envelope are viral glycoprotein spikes that play a crucial role in host cell recognition, attachment, and subsequent membrane fusion, thereby initiating infection. These surface glycoproteins are essential determinants of viral tropism and pathogenicity (Figure 2) (36). The hantavirus genome is composed of three segments of negative-sense, single-stranded RNA, designated as the large (L), medium (M), and small (S) segments. Each segment encodes specific viral proteins that are essential for the replication cycle and structural integrity of the virion. The L segment encodes the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), which is responsible for transcription and replication of the viral genome. The M segment encodes the precursor of the envelope glycoproteins Gn and Gc, which are later processed and incorporated into the viral envelope to mediate host cell entry. The S segment encodes the nucleocapsid (N) protein, which binds and encapsidates viral RNA, forming ribonucleoprotein complexes that protect the genome from degra- dation and are essential for replication and transcription (37). Beyond its structural role, the nucleocapsid protein also con- tributes to immune evasion by interfering with host innate immune responses. Importantly, the segmented nature of the hantavirus genome allows for genetic reassortment when multiple strains co-infect the same host cell. This mechanism significantly enhances viral genetic diversity and plays a key role in the emergence of novel strains with altered virulence, host range, and epidemiological characteristics (36, 37). Molecular biology and replication cycle Viral attachment and entry Hantaviruses exhibit a broad cellular tropism, with primary infection occurring in endothelial cells, macrophages, dendritic cells, and epithelial cells. This tropism is a key determinant of disease pathology, particularly the vascular dysfunction observed in hantavirus-associated syndromes. full_text_sections.full_text: Hantaviruses at an inflection point: scientific evidence, spillover risk, and One Health approach Ilyes Zatla * Independent Researcher, Tlemcen, Algeria Hantaviruses are zoonotic RNA viruses that cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome and are primarily main- tained in rodent reservoirs. Transmission to humans occurs mainly by inhalation of aerosolized excreta from infected rodents, but Andes virus uniquely shows documented limited person-to-person spread with important clinical and public- health implications. Environmental change, urbanization, and global mobility have broadened hantavirus geographic risk and contributed to recent multi-country clusters, including expedition cruise-ship–associated events that highlighted preparedness gaps. This review synthesizes current knowledge on hantavirus taxonomy, molecular biology, transmission pathways, host reservoirs, pathogen- esis, clinical features, diagnostics, and management, and it critically assesses advances in molecular surveillance, phylogenetics, antiviral research, and emerg- ing nanobiotechnological approaches. I operationalize a One Health framework into concrete prevention and control actions, integrated human–animal–envi- ronment surveillance, targeted rodent reservoir monitoring and control, environ- mental sampling, and formal intersectoral coordination mechanisms, and I map epidemiologic findings to prioritized, group-specific public-health interventions. Finally, I identify current controversies and knowledge gaps (reservoir compe- tence, surveillance sensitivity, and limits of predictive models), and propose a research and policy agenda to strengthen global preparedness for high-conse- quence hantavirus events. KEYWORDS disease transmission, epidemiology, Hantavirus, one health, physiopathology, therapeutics, zoonosis Introduction Hantaviruses are zoonotic pathogens that represent one of the most significant rodent- borne viral threats to human health. They are distributed worldwide and are associated with two major clinical syndromes: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), predom- inantly observed in Europe and Asia, and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), mainly reported in the Americas. These diseases differ in clinical presentation and mortality but share common virological and ecological characteristics (1, 2). The discovery of hantaviruses dates back to the Korean War during the early 1950s, when thousands of United Nations soldiers developed a severe febrile illness later identified as Korean hemorrhagic fever.
